body: If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken. While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk. TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first. According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans. The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay. That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system. The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers. If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. body: Tokenized equities are still far too small to move BTC or ETH. The read-through is for listed crypto names tied to the sector, including Robinhood as an issuer and Coinbase as a venue for tokenized assets, and for the wider real-world asset story. If Nvidia’s post-earnings gains hold, most of the tokens minted near $156 will be in profit. That would help issuers argue that onchain demand rises with volatility instead of evaporating. The risk is redemptions into strength, which would shrink supply as quickly as it grew and weaken the case for tokenized stocks as a lasting home for retail risk appetite. While Wall Street sold Nvidia’s leadership crisis, onchain buyers minted more than a million new tokenized shares, and Kress’s first earnings beat gave them an early reason to feel good about it. Holders of tokenized Nvidia stock added to their positions as the chipmaker’s shares fell through the week of Jensen Huang’s resignation, with onchain supply rising 121% to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations. Over the same seven days, Nvidia’s share price dropped 13% to around $156. The timing also stands out. The data show supply starting to climb around November 9 and 10, after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on November 8 and before the November 12 announcement that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and director. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones became the company’s first board chair. Most of the new supply came through bStocks’ NVDAb token, with xStocks’ NVDAx, Robinhood’s version and 15 smaller tokens making up the rest. Those buyers got an early test of their conviction overnight. As we reported, Kress’s first quarterly report since Huang’s departure topped forecasts by about $7 billion, and she pointed to a $2.5 trillion backlog while guiding for revenue growth of around 75% next year. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading. The episode offers a rare look at how onchain equity holders behave during a single-stock shock. The sums are small beside Nvidia’s market value of several trillion dollars, but the direction is clear: demand for tokenized exposure rose as the price fell. The next few sessions will show whether that was conviction or a short-term trade. If supply holds or keeps growing after the post-earnings bounce, issuers will have evidence that volatility brings in buyers. If holders redeem into strength, the surge will look more like a quick dip trade than a lasting shift. as a ps. if there is any demand for it I'll post up a separate explainer on all this. body: The Australian dollar barely moved, holding around 0.67, because traders treated the data as backward-looking and are focused on Thursday’s jobs report. Swaps still lean towards a peak in rates. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. Watch the jobless rate on Thursday more closely than the headline jobs figure. --- Australia now has wages, interest rates and unemployment all rising together, which leaves the RBA choosing between the pay data and the layoff headlines. Australian wages grew at their fastest pace in nearly three years in the September quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to keep policy tight even as cracks appear in the jobs market. The Australian Bureau of Statistics said its wage price index rose 1.1% in the quarter, the strongest result since late 2023. That broke a run of five quarters at around 0.8% and topped forecasts of between 0.9% and 1.0%. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%. Private sector pay rose 3.4% over the year and public sector pay 3.9%, Reuters reported. The ABS pointed to two drivers. The Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase in minimum and award wages from July lifted private sector pay, while raises for state government frontline workers pushed up public sector wages. Public sector pay has now outpaced the private sector for seven straight quarters. Real wages are still going backwards, down 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of decline. For the RBA, the harder question is what it may take to bring inflation down. If pay keeps rising at this rate, the bank may have to tolerate a jobless rate higher than it currently projects, possibly above the level it regards as consistent with steady inflation. The central bank has argued that the labour market is easing, yet pay growth shows little sign of cooling broadly. And unless productivity picks up, wage gains of this size sit uneasily with inflation returning to the 2% to 3% band. For households, at least, bigger pay rises offer some relief after a long squeeze. The bank lifted rates for a fifth time this year in November, to an 18-year high of 4.85%, partly because it judged the labour market to be a little tight. Three board members opposed the move, concerned the economy could be heading for a materially sharper downturn. One economist noted that Australia is in the unusual position of having unemployment, interest rates and wages all rising at once, and said wage growth and joblessness are likely to stay elevated through 2027. There are signs that the labour market is weakening. Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.7% in September, and layoffs are spreading. Department store David Jones plans to cut 1,500 jobs by the end of the year, and hardware chain Bunnings said this week it would cut around 230 permanent roles. That puts Thursday’s employment report in focus. Forecasts point to a rise of 25,000 jobs in October and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.7%. Markets largely looked through the wage figures, treating them as backward-looking. Swaps still imply about a 75% chance that the RBA has finished raising rates, with roughly 20 basis points of easing priced by the end of 2027. body: Record exports support the view that Japan’s economy can absorb a December rate hike despite the third-quarter contraction, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. Chipmakers and chip equipment suppliers in Tokyo are the clearest beneficiaries, though the reliance on AI demand leaves them exposed to any pullback in global tech spending. Oil is the swing factor for the trade balance: crude prices tied to the Iran war set the size of Japan’s import bill, and a renewed spike would quickly widen the deficit. The yen is likely to take its direction from US-Japan rate gaps rather than the trade figures. --- Japan is selling more than ever to an AI-hungry world, but record oil-driven import costs mean households are not sharing in the boom. Japan’s exports rose for a 14th straight month in October and hit a record value, as global investment in artificial intelligence kept demand for chip-related shipments strong, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Exports climbed 20.5% from a year earlier to about ¥11.8 trillion, roughly $74 billion and the highest for any single month on record, Reuters reported. That beat the 20% median forecast and picked up from September’s 16.5% gain. Shipments to the United States rose about 24%, while exports to China increased about 13%. Analysts cited by Reuters said AI-related demand continued to support exports of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, helping offset sluggish Chinese demand. Economists also noted that companies passing on higher costs had lifted the nominal value of shipments, so part of the gain reflects prices rather than volumes. Imports also set a monthly record at about ¥12.2 trillion, up 21.6% from a year earlier, although that was below the 25.8% forecast. Elevated crude prices and higher transport costs pushed up the value of energy imports amid instability in the Middle East, even as import volumes slipped 0.2%. Oil remains Japan’s main exposure to the Iran war, since the country imports close to 90% of its energy. The softer than expected import bill left a trade deficit of around ¥477 billion, about half the shortfall economists had forecast. The data shows external demand is still supporting an economy that contracted unexpectedly in the third quarter, as higher living costs forced households to cut spending. Rising import costs are likely to keep squeezing household purchasing power and corporate margins, which means the export boom is not translating into broad domestic strength. For the Bank of Japan, the figures add to the case for raising rates in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, and that financial conditions remain accommodative. The policy rate is 1.25%. Resilient exports help offset the weak GDP reading, while import-driven inflation keeps pressure on the bank to act. The yen has drawn little support so far. USD/JPY remains near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention, as the rate gap with a Federal Reserve on a hiking path dominates. The risks to the export run are a slowdown in AI investment and further escalation in the Middle East, which would lift the oil import bill again. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The narrower deficit is mildly supportive for the yen because it reduces the yen sold to pay for imports. Rate differentials still dominate, though, and USD/JPY remains pinned near 160 while the Fed is on a hiking path. Oil is the key swing factor: Japan’s import bill is highly sensitive to crude prices during the Iran war, so any renewed rise in oil would quickly reverse today’s improvement. For the BOJ, the data adds to evidence that the economy can absorb a December hike, which could nudge short-end JGB yields higher. Exporters with heavy chip exposure should find support in Tokyo trade. Chips lifted Japan’s exports and a lighter import bill halved the expected trade gap, but the yen is still taking its cue from Washington, not Tokyo. Japan’s exports rose 20.5% in October from a year earlier, slightly ahead of expectations and a clear pick-up from September’s revised 16.5%, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Chip shipments led the gain, ending a two-month slowdown in export growth. Imports rose 21.6%, well short of forecasts of about 26%, after an 18.5% rise in September. As a result, the trade deficit came in at around ¥477 billion. That was roughly half the ¥1 trillion or so analysts had expected and narrower than September’s revised ¥557 billion. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the deficit was around ¥767 billion, smaller than forecast but wider than the previous month. The import figure is the surprise. The government had said crude procurement would recover in October to around year-earlier levels as tankers routed through the Suez Canal arrived, so a bigger jump in the import bill was widely expected. Energy is Japan’s main vulnerability in the Iran war. The country imports close to 90% of its energy, and high oil prices have kept its import bill elevated. The data adds a modest tailwind to the Bank of Japan’s case for raising rates in December. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, but Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled strong prospects for a hike at the next meeting after declaring that underlying inflation had reached the 2% target. Board member Hajime Takata said this week that rates should rise nimbly. Solid exports help offset a slight contraction in third-quarter GDP, and a narrower trade deficit means fewer yen are being sold to pay for imports. That may not be enough to lift the yen on its own. USD/JPY is trading around 159.5, just below the 160 level where Tokyo has stepped up warnings about intervention. With the Federal Reserve on a hiking path and US 10-year yields above 5%, the rate gap still works against the yen even if the Bank of Japan hikes. The 10-year JGB yield is near 2.9%, close to its highest since late October. The next test is Friday’s national inflation data. A firm reading alongside today’s trade figures would strengthen expectations for a December move. A rise in oil prices, on the other hand, would quickly push the import bill and the deficit back up. body: U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, its highest level in a year, as fuel costs continued to rise. The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%. Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated. The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022. Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996. The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July. Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027. Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside." Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Bank of England's final meeting of the year. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the release that a recent climb down in oil prices following the U.S. midterm elections could offer some relief in future inflation readings. But he added: "While this may be a short-term reprieve for motorists, the broader outlook for UK inflation remains challenging as we approach 2027. After hiking interest rates at the start of the month, the Bank will be wary of a sustained uptick in inflation that could be here to stay."

title: Economists see no November interest rate hike as fuel prices offer relief - thenational.co.za
body: South African economists expect the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) to keep interest rates unchanged at its November Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting on Thursday, despite expectations that inflation will climb above 5% in October. The repo rate currently stands at 7.25%, following the Reserve Bank's previous increase. While rising petrol prices and a weaker rand have renewed concerns about inflation, economists believe falling international oil prices and the prospect of lower domestic fuel costs could ease price pressures in the months ahead. Frank Blackmore, lead economist at KPMG South Africa, said the MPC faced competing considerations ahead of its announcement. October inflation is expected to increase significantly from September's 4.5%, partly because of the sharp petrol price increases during the month. International developments and pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates could also influence the Reserve Bank's decision. However, Blackmore said the recent decline in oil prices had reduced some of the inflationary risks. He pointed to fuel price over-recoveries of approximately R3 per litre, suggesting that motorists could see a reduction of around R3 per litre in December. Although October's inflation reading could be higher, softer fuel prices could help bring inflation down in November and December, before it continues to moderate through 2027. Blackmore said the Reserve Bank would also need to consider the pressure already facing consumers from rising living costs. “I believe we could see the Bank hold rates at its November meeting and reassess the position at its January meeting next year,” he said. Dr Lerato Ntuli, economist at Anchor Capital, also expects the MPC to leave the repo rate unchanged at 7.25%. She said the balance of risks remained tilted towards another increase rather than an immediate rate cut, but the likelihood of a further hike had diminished over the past month. September headline inflation came in at 4.5% year on year, below market expectations, while core inflation eased to 4%, suggesting underlying price pressures remained relatively contained. Ntuli expects October inflation to accelerate because of fuel price pressures, but said the outlook beyond that had become more favourable. Government fuel levy relief , together with the decline in Brent crude prices from around $130 a barrel at the end of October to approximately $92 currently, could place downward pressure on inflation in November and December. Johann Els, chief economist at PSG Financial Services, also expects the Reserve Bank to keep rates unchanged, although he anticipates a relatively hawkish statement and the possibility of a split vote. Els expects October consumer price inflation to rise from 4.5% in September to approximately 5.2%, reflecting a monthly increase of around 0.7%. The biggest contributor is expected to be petrol prices, which increased by 320 cents per litre in October this year, compared with an increase of just 8 cents in October 2025. He said food inflation and prices across several consumer goods categories remained relatively subdued, with little evidence so far of higher fuel costs feeding through into the wider consumer price basket. Els expects inflation to remain above 5% in November and December, potentially reaching around 5.3%, before moderating during 2027. His average inflation forecast is 4.3% for 2026 and 3.4% for 2027. While management reaffirmed support for vital AI infrastructure partners, Nvidia is tightening counterparty evaluation and credit standards, shifting toward a capital allocation strategy that prioritizes high demand visibility and credit quality. Neo-cloud companies such as CoreWeave, IREN, and Nebius primarily generate revenue by building data centers, purchasing Nvidia GPUs, and leasing computing power to customers. Compared with tech giants that have mature cloud businesses, such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, these firms have smaller balance sheets and rely more heavily on bonds, loans, and external equity financing for expansion. As data center construction costs and borrowing rates rise, the market has begun to worry that neo-cloud companies' growth could outpace their financing capacity. Investors are also concerned that following Jensen Huang's departure, Nvidia's new management could cut investments, credit guarantees, and purchase commitments to related companies, thereby leading to data center delays and a slowdown in GPU orders. Kress's comments on the earnings call eased this concern. She noted that neo-cloud providers have become an increasingly vital part of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem, helping startups, model developers, sovereign clients, and traditional enterprises access Nvidia computing power while expanding the reach of the Nvidia platform. Kress acknowledged that neo-cloud companies and frontier model labs face exceptionally strong compute demand, but the expansion pace of some firms has already outpaced their balance sheets and long-term credit capacity. If partners fail to meet these conditions, the actual amounts and timing assumed by Nvidia will be adjusted accordingly. The company will prioritize data center projects with high demand visibility that can support multiple generations of computing platforms. US AI chip giant Nvidia reported another blockbuster quarter in FY27, with revenue more than doubling year-on-year to $115.8 billion in Q3. In its first earnings report following Jensen Huang's exit as CEO, management sought to reassure investors, saying it was "business as usual". The stock, which has plunged nearly 29 percent since reports surrounding the affair scandal surfaced, was trading about 4 percent higher in after-hours trade following the results. Analysts believe the stock looks attractive from a medium- to long-term perspective, as the company raises its revenue outlook for Q4 and FY28. Peter McGuire, Chief Strategist - Asia-Pac at XM.com, said Nvidia's Q3 numbers were a "ball out of the park", with earnings per share (EPS) at $2.68 against estimates of $2.40. "The stock has seen a sharp fall from October peaks and the stock cannot hide given its strong earnings profile. The company's sales guidance revision to 75 percent from 70 percent for FY28 is also quite strong, and 2027 will be an interesting year to watch the stock since it has already seen such a sharp plunge," he said. In Q3, net income rose 105 percent year-on-year to $65.3 billion, while operating income increased 115 percent to $77.5 billion. Data centre revenue hit a record $107.6 billion, up 110 percent year-on-year, while edge computing revenue rose 42 percent to $8.2 billion. Gross margin stood at 74.8 percent, compared with 73.4 percent in Q3FY26. Looking ahead, interim CEO Colette Kress said revenue is expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3 percent, in Q4FY27, with the quarter also expected to mark a bottom in margins. For FY28, management raised its sales growth forecast to 75 percent year-on-year from the earlier estimate of 70 percent. Gross margins are expected to improve to between 72 percent and 73 percent. Addressing Jensen Huang's exit, the board said it does not plan to reinstate him as chief executive and has retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to identify a permanent CEO. The latest reports surrounding the affair have added to pressure on a stock that was already witnessing a sharp selloff amid the unwinding of the AI trade. From its October 6 peak, Nvidia has fallen 35 percent and is down 17 percent year-to-date. At current levels, McGuire said the stock offers a compelling buying opportunity. "We can see some softness in the stock over the near term due to several factors like inflation concerns in the US and dollar movement.
